The issues were severe enough that the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) advised organizations using PHP on their systems to either immediately update or take their systems offline until they could.

But the PHP update wasn’t the only headache cybersecurity folks were facing on Wednesday. Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment, also dropped a security surprise of its own when it shared that four high-severity vulnerabilities were just patched in its latest release. One allowed remote code execution, and two others would have permitted a TLS validation bypass, potentially allowing attackers to bypass checks intended to verify a server’s identity.

by:

![Lizz Parody](https://assets.nodesource.com/strapi-uploads/avatar-liz-parody_801de3cda8.jpg)[Lizz Parody](/blog/author/liz-parody)

in [Node.js](/blog/category/node-js-1)  on Nov 08 2024

* [Community](/blog/tag/community "Community")

* [ESM](/blog/tag/esm "ESM")

* [Node.js](/blog/tag/node-js-1 "Node.js")

On October 29, 2024,\*\* Node.js v22 \*\*officially transitioned into **Long Term Support (LTS)** with the codename **'Jod'**.

For developers and organizations relying on the stability of Node.js for production environments, this transition marks a key milestone for Node.js 22.x, ensuring it will receive critical updates and security support for years to come.

Let’s take a closer look at what this means, along with a refresher on the Node.js release lifecycle 🔄.

> I believe the transition to LTS makes this release line more stable, especially given the improvements made over 10 releases.
